narrative: The model estimated a 53.1% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this is slightly above the threshold used for this decision, your application was rejected. This is a probabilistic judgment, not a certainty, and it was driven mainly by three factors. The strongest influence was your third-year class rank: you were in the fourth decile, below the average of about the sixth decile among accepted students, and this pushed the prediction toward failure. The second factor was your family-income bracket; being in the upper-middle bracket contributed mildly toward the failure prediction in the model’s assessment, even though upper-middle is the largest accepted group at 45.4%. The third factor, your LSAT score of 30, was below the accepted-student average of about 37, yet in this particular prediction it was the only top factor that pushed toward passing; its favorable effect was not enough to overcome the other signals. To improve your chances, focus on what you can change: strengthen your academic record, especially upper-level law-related coursework, and seek advising on how to address your third-year rank. If your practice scores suggest meaningful improvement, consider retaking the LSAT. Because 53.1% is close to the dividing line, a stronger revised application or a later application cycle could materially change the outcome.
